السابق لوزارة الخارجية في الخرطوم الخرطوم 1 نوفمبر 2026- أودعت الحكومة السودانية شكوى ضد إثيوبيا لدى كل من مجلس الأمن الدولي ومجلس السلم والأمن الإفريقي، على خلفية اتهامات لأديس أبابا بالتورط في الاعتداء على مواقع وأعيان مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في عدد من ولايات السودان، ما تسبب في وقوع ضحايا مدنيين وتعطيل للخدمات الضرورية. وقالت وزارة الخارجية السودانية في بيان، الأحد، إن “حكومة السودان أرفقت كافة الوثائق والمستندات التي تؤكد استخدام الدعم السريع للأراضي الإثيوبية لإطلاق المسيرات الانتحارية والمزودة بالصواريخ، مستهدفة الأعيان المدنية والمرافق الحيوية”. وعلى مدى أسبوع، تواجه محطات الكهرباء في معظم أنحاء السودان استهدافاً ممنهجاً بالمسيرات، حيث تعرضت أكثر من 14 محطة لتوزيع الكهرباء في ولايات القضارف والخرطوم والجزيرة والبحر الأحمر، فضلاً عن سنار والنيل الأبيض وجنوب كردفان ونهر النيل والشمالية، لهجمات وأضرار بالغة تسببت في انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن عدد من المدن. وتقول الحكومة السودانية إن المسيرات تنطلق من قواعد في إثيوبيا، سمت منها قاعدتي أصوصا وبحر دار، كما تقول إن هذه المواقع تُستخدم لتزويد المليشيا بالسلاح والعتاد وتسهيل مرور المقاتلين الأجانب المرتزقة الذين يشاركون في العدوان على السودان، علاوة على أنها منصات لإطلاق المسيرات صوب العمق السوداني. وشدد بيان الخارجية السودانية على أن استخدام الدعم السريع للأراضي الإثيوبية لاستهداف السودان يُعد عملاً عدائياً يضع إثيوبيا أمام القانون الدولي، ويحاسبها على انتهاكها للمادة (4) 2 من ميثاق الأمم المتحدة. وطالبت حكومة السودان نظيرتها الإثيوبية بوقف هذه الأعمال العدائية، كما حثت المجتمع الدولي على القيام بدوره تجاه محاسبة “المليشيا الإرهابية” وتطبيق القانون الدولي على الحكومة الإثيوبية. الكلمات: أزمة الكهرباء مقالات | رأي ما هي طبيعة شعار الحسم العسكري لحرب السودان؟ منذ ساعة واحدة د. الشفيع خضر سعيد حجم الخط 0 تفاعل عدد كبير من القراء مع ما جاء في المقالين السابقين، ولم يبخلوا بإرسال ملاحظاتهم وتعليقاتهم، وبعضهم أرسل مساهمة كاملة، فلهم جميعا مني كل الشكر والتقدير. في نهاية هذه السلسلة من المقالات، سألخص وأنشر كل ما وصلني، وسيصلني، من القراء الكرام. نواصل المناقشة حول السؤالين المطروحين في مقالنا السابق: هل يمكن حسم حرب السودان عسكريا؟ وما هو البديل العملي عن انتظار الحسم العسكري؟ في البدء، أعتقد بضرورة فصل سؤال القدرة التقنية لأي من أطراف النزاع على تحقيق انتصار ميداني وحسم الحرب، عن السؤال الأعمق والأخطر المتعلق بماهية طبيعة شعار الحسم العسكري؟ هل يُقرأ الشعار دائماً كخطة عمليات عسكرية ومجرد أداة عسكرية طارئة لحسم النزاع، أم تحول إلى رؤية سياسية واستراتيجية حول مستقبل الدولة السودانية؟ بمعنى، هل يكتفي شعار الحسم العسكري بكونه استراتيجية قابلة للتحقيق ينحصر هدفها في إنهاء الحرب، أم أنه تخطى ذلك الهدف ليصبح، لدى بعض القوى، تصور سياسي يتعلق بمستقبل السودان يجري تقديمه في صورة هدف عسكري بحت؟ أعتقد أن هذا السؤال يستحق نقاشًا عميقًا، وأدعو القراء إلى الإدلاء بدلوهم فيه. ومن جانبي أساهم بالنقاط التالية: أولا، نكرر ما ناقشناه في مقالنا السابق، من أن فكرة الحسم العسكري للحرب في السودان، تظل إمكانية نظرية فقط، إذ تواجهها تحديات وتعقيدات هيكلية بالغة، تجعل تحقيق هذه الفكرة أقرب إلى الاستحالة. وفي مقدمة هذه التحديات والتعقيدات، طبيعة الحرب غير المتماثلة، أو غير المتجانسة، بين طرفين تتباين قدراتهم المادية بشكل صارخ: جيش نظامي تقليدي في مواجهة جماعات وتشكيلات مسلحة غير نظامية، وعابرة للحدود والقبائل، ينقصها العتاد العسكري التقليدي لكنها تستطيع تعويضه باللجوء إلى تكتيكات غير تقليدية كحرب المدن والهجمات المباغتة، أو حرب عصابات. وإذا أضفنا إلى ذلك هشاشة البنيان المؤسسي وتآكل الدولة بعد ثلاثة عقود عجاف تحت قبضة الإنقاذ، والدعم الخارجي المستمر، فإن بوصلة الحرب ستتجه أكثر نحو انسداد سياسي طويل الأمد، وصراع استنزافي، وليس نصرًا سريعًا لأي من الطرفين في ساحة المعركة. وقد تتحول الحرب في نهاية المطاف إلى شكل من أشكال الجمود العسكري أو التقسيم الفعلي. من ناحية أخرى، حتى إذا افترضنا قدرة أحد الطرفين على إحراز نصر عسكري ساحق، فإن الثمن سيكون انهيار ما تبقى من بنى تحتية ومؤسسات وطنية، وتشريد ملايين إضافيين، وتعميق الشرخ الاجتماعي والجهوي بما يعرقل أي بناء مستقبلي للدولة. فكرة الحسم العسكري للحرب في السودان، تظل إمكانية نظرية فقط، إذ تواجهها تحديات وتعقيدات هيكلية بالغة، تجعل تحقيق هذه الفكرة أقرب إلى الاستحالة ثانيا، أعتقد أن الإصرار على رفع شعار الحسم العسكري لدى بعض الأطراف يمكن أن يُقرأ كتصور سياسي مُقنّع في غطاء عسكري، أي غالباً ما يُفسر باعتباره أجندة سياسية ومستقبلية يجري تسويقها في قالب عسكري تعبوي! فبالنسبة لهذه الأطراف والقوى السياسية المتحالفة أو الداعمة لخيارات استمرار الحرب، فإن شعار الحسم العسكري قد تجاوز دلالته التكتيكية البحتة ليصبح مشروعاً سياسياً لمستقبل الدولة، ووسيلة لإقصاء الخصوم والتيارات المناوئة، سواء كانوا سياسيين أو عسكريين أو مجموعات قاعدية، ومحاولة لفرض رؤية أحادية للشكل القادم للسلطة. ثالثا، البعض قد يرى في خطاب الحسم العسكري وسيلة للهروب من مسار العملية السياسية، وأداة تعفيه من خوض تسوية صعبة مع الأطراف الأخرى، وتقديم تنازلات مؤلمة. رابعا، في ظل مشاعر الغضب والاستقطاب الحاد، يُقدَّم شعار الحسم العسكري كرمز لـكرامة الدولة وسيادتها المهددة. إنه يعبر عن رغبة وجدانية لدى قطاعات واسعة من الشعب السوداني المقهور في رؤية نهاية حاسمة لمن تسبب في معاناتهم، مما يجعله خطاباً شعبوياً جذاباً بغض النظر عن تعقيداته على الأرض. خلاصة حديثنا حول السؤال الأعمق والأخطر المتعلق بماهية طبيعة شعار الحسم العسكري، أن الحرب الدائرة اليوم في السودان من المستبعد أن تحسم عسكريا. والمنطق التاريخي لتجارب الحروب الأهلية في العالم يقول إن الحسم العسكري قد ينهي معركة، لكنه لا يحسم بالضرورة الحرب أو الصراع، وهو قطعا يعجز عن بناء الوطن. وكما أشرنا في مقالنا السابق، فإن المعيار الحقيقي ليس فقط في الحسم العسكري ومَن يسيطر على الأرض، بل ما إذا كان السودانيون سيتمكنون بعد ذلك الحسم وتلك السيطرة من العيش في دولة لا يحتاجون فيها إلى السلاح لحماية أنفسهم أو انتزاع حقوقهم. إن أي استقرار مستدام في السودان سيتطلب في نهاية المطاف، وقبل أو بعد أي مآلات ميدانية عسكرية، تسوية سياسية وطنية شاملة تُعيد تعريف عقد الاجتماع السوداني وتؤسس لدولة القانون والمؤسسات التي لا تقبل الاحتكار ولا الإقصاء. ننتقل الآن للإجابة على السؤال المتعلق بالبديل العملي عن انتظار الحسم العسكري. وكمدخل لمناقشة هذا السؤال، نرصد العوامل المرجّحة لإنهاء الحرب، وبعضها ينضج طبيعيا، والبعض الآخر يتطلب إرادة قوية لإنضاجه وتفعيله. أحد هذه العوامل، والذي ينضج طبيعيا مع مرور الزمن، هو حالة الإنهاك وتوازن الضعف التي تصيب أطراف النزاع. هذه الحالة تنضج وتتحقق عندما يصل الوضع إلى نقطة تدرك فيها الاطراف المتقاتلة عدم قدرة أي منها على تحقيق حسم عسكري كامل على الأرض، وأن تكلفة استمرار الحرب باتت أعلى من تكلفة الجلوس إلى طاولة المفاوضات. أما العوامل التي تحتاج إلى إرادة قوية لإنضاجها وتفعيلها، ففي مقدمتها تشكيل جبهة مدنية سودانية واسعة قادرة على ملء الفراغ السياسي وفرض رؤية للتحول المدني، بما يمنع استئثار القوى المسلحة بإدارة مستقبَل البلاد. وقادرة أيضا على إسماع الصوت المدني للمجتمعين الدولي والإقليمي حتى تتوحد إرادتهما بهدف فرض جبهة موحدة لوقف تدفق السلاح والدعم الإمدادي والمساندة من قوى إقليمية ودولية متعددة، ويضغط مباشرة نحو إنهاء المعارك. وأيضا بهدف توحيد المنابر الدولية والإقليمية لفرض وقف إطلاق النار، وبآليات تنفيذية وضغوط دولية جادة. ونستكمل الإجابة على سؤال البديل في مقالنا القادم. ٭ كاتب سوداني كلمات مفتاحية د. الشفيع خضر سعيد اترك تعليقاً إلغاء في السودان. وتسببت الحرب في السودان التي اندلعت منتصف أبريل 2023م في دمار هائل طال القطاع الصناعي والمصانع، حيث يُقدَّر إجمالي خسائر القطاع بعشرات المليارات من الدولارات مع خروج معظم المنشآت عن الخدمة. وبحسب بيان صحفي، فإن «زويال القابضة» السودانية وقعت اتفاقية لإنشاء أربعة مصانع اقتصادية جديدة مع شركة «الجيد بن سعود» السعودية في قطاعات إنتاجية مختلفة داخل السودان، بهدف تعزيز التنمية الصناعية ودعم السوق المحلي بالمنتجات الأساسية. وتتضمن الاتفاقية إنشاء أربعة مصانع تشمل: مصنعاً للأسمنت، وآخر للمواد الغذائية، ومصنعاً لإنتاج بطاريات الليثيوم أيون، إلى جانب مصنع لتجميع وإنتاج السيارات الكهربائية. ووفقاً للبيانات الأولية للمشروع، ستعتمد المصانع على الاستفادة من المواد الخام المحلية وتوظيف تقنيات إنتاج حديثة، بما يسهم في خفض تكاليف الاستيراد، وتعزيز الإنتاج الوطني، وتقليل الاعتماد على المنتجات المستوردة. وأوضح البيان أن الاتفاقية تأتي في إطار مساعي القطاع الخاص لزيادة القدرات الإنتاجية، وتوفير فرص عمل جديدة، والمساهمة في تلبية احتياجات السوق المحلي، في ظل التحديات الاقتصادية الراهنة. وحددت الاتفاقية الفترة من الأول من ديسمبر 2026م وحتى يناير 2030م لتنفيذ المشروع وإنشاء المصانع الأربعة. من جانبه، أبدى مجلس إدارة شركة «الجيد بن سعود» اهتماماً بتعزيز التعاون المشترك، مؤكداً خسائر بشرية واستهداف مرافق حيوية بحسب التقرير السوداني، أوقعت الهجمات 484 مدنيًا بين قتيل ومصاب، فضلًا عن مقتل 176 مجنّدًا في الجيش. وطالت الخرطوم والنيل الأزرق ومناطق أخرى، مستهدفة مستشفيات وأحياء سكنية ومنشآت للوقود والكهرباء. ومن بين الوقائع التي أوردها التقرير، هجوم استهدف عائلات نازحة في منطقة ود الماحي بولاية النيل الأزرق الشهر الماضي، وأدى إلى مقتل 30 مدنيًا، هم 26 امرأة وأربعة أطفال. الذي أعدّته وزارة الخارجية السودانية بالتعاون مع الاستخبارات العسكرية والعامة، إلى فحص حطام الطائرات المسيّرة وبيانات رحلاتها والسجلات العسكرية. وأشار إلى العثور على حاسوب تحكّم تابع لإحدى المسيّرات التي سقطت في الدمازين بولاية النيل الأزرق في أيلول. وبحسب التقرير، احتوى الحاسوب على بيانات لمسار الطائرة تُظهر انطلاقها من موقع يبعد 1.7 كيلومتر داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية. وانطلاقًا من هذه المعطيات، التقرير أن السودان يسعى إلى "المساءلة والحصول على تعويضات عن الأضرار والدمار الناجم عن تلك الأعمال". الأحد، إن القوات المسلحة ماضية في التوجه إلى إقليمي دارفور وكردفان لقتال من وصفهم بالمرتزقة، وإحباط مؤامرات دولة الإمارات العربية المتحدة وجهاز الموساد الإسرائيلي. وتتهم الحكومة السودانية الإمارات بشكل متكرر بدعم وتزويد قوات الدعم السريع بالأسلحة والمساعدات العسكرية والتورط المباشر في استهداف المدنيين والبنى التحتية عن طريق الطائرات المسيّرة، لكن أباظبي ظلت تنفي هذه الاتهامات وتؤكد سعيها لدعم وقف إطلاق النار وحل الأزمة سياسياً وتسهيل المساعدات الإنسانية. وقال العطا لدى مخاطبته مجموعة من القوات المرابطة في الخرطوم: “نحن ذاهبون إلى دارفور وكردفان لقتال آلاف المرتزقة القادمين من غرب إفريقيا وإثيوبيا وكولومبيا وجنوب السودان، الذين جلبهم محمد بن زايد.. نقاتل من أجل إحباط مؤامرات دولة الشر ومشروع أبناء زايد والموساد”. وشدد على أن حرب القوات المسلحة ليست ضد قبيلة أو مجتمعات جغرافية محددة، مبيناً أن كل قبائل دارفور وكردفان “عزيزة”. وأضاف بقوله: “لسنا ذاهبين لقتال الرزيقات والحوازمة والهبانية والبني هلبة، ولا نريد أن ننتقم كما فعلت المليشيا ضد مواطني أقاليم السودان المختلفة، نحن ذاهبون لنقاتل المرتزقة”. وأكد العطا أنٌ استهداف الكهرباء والبنية التحتية لن يثني عن المضي نحو هزيمة “التمرد” وتحرير كل شبرٍ من اراضي السودان، مضيفاً أنُ هذا الاستهداف يمثل الدافع والسبب لتطوير البنية التحتية وتعزيز الخدمات بواسطة الحكومة. ويسعى الجيش السوداني إلى التقدم نحو إقليم دارفور الذي تسيطر قوات الدعم السريع على الجزء الأكبر من أراضيه، بالتزامن مع مساعيه لاستكمال سيطرته على ما تبقى من مناطق إقليم كردفان. وخلال الأشهر الثلاثة الماضية، تمكن الجيش والقوات المتحالفة معه من استعادة مناطق واسعة في كردفان، بما في ذلك طرق إمداد رئيسية كانت تستخدمها قوات الدعم السريع لربط مواقعها في الإقليم بقواتها في دارفور، ما أدى إلى تغيير في خريطة السيطرة العسكرية في إقليم كردفان. الكلمات: التطورات العسكرية في السودان الجيش السوداني الخرطوم الدعم السريع حرب السودان دارفور كردفان ياسر العطا مقالات ذات صلة بدء الصورة: ASHRAF SHAZLY / AFP الخرطوم 1 نوفمبر 2026 – أغلقت عشرات المخابز في العاصمة السودانية أبوابها بسبب شح الدقيق وانقطاع الكهرباء وندرة الجازولين، ما فاقم معاناة المواطنين في الحصول على الخبز. وتشهد العاصمة الخرطوم وعدد من الولايات أزمات متكررة في الوقود والمواصلات، إلى جانب نقص الخبز، الأمر الذي دفع العديد من الأسر إلى اللجوء لبدائل أخرى لتوفير احتياجاتها اليومية. وكشف نائب رئيس اتحاد المخابز، عصام عكاشة، لـ «سودان تربيون»، الأحد، عن تفاقم أزمة الخبز في ولاية الخرطوم بصورة حادة، مشيراً إلى إغلاق عدد من المخابز أبوابها نتيجة شح الدقيق والجازولين والانقطاع المتكرر للتيار الكهربائي، ما انعكس على حجم الإنتاج واستمرارية العمل. وقال عكاشة إن أزمة الجازولين تمثل أحد أبرز التحديات التي تواجه المخابز، موضحاً أن المخابز تعتمد على الوقود في تشغيل المولدات، في ظل عدم استقرار الإمداد الكهربائي، الأمر الذي أدى إلى توقف عدد كبير منها، لا سيما في المناطق الريفية. وأشار إلى أن الحصص المخصصة للمطاحن غير منتظمة، مبيناً أن المطاحن نفسها تعاني انخفاضاً في حجم الإنتاج، ولا تتلقى حصصاً ثابتة من القمح، إذ تتفاوت فترات الإمداد بين يوم وآخر، وقد تمتد أحياناً إلى أسبوع، ما يجعل توفير الدقيق للمخابز أمراً صعباً. ويُقدَّر استهلاك مخابز العاصمة الخرطوم من الدقيق بنحو 45 ألف جوال زنة 50 كيلوغراماً يومياً. وفيما يتعلق بعدد المخابز التي أغلقت أبوابها، أوضح عكاشة أنه لا يستطيع تحديد العدد بصورة دقيقة، لعدم توفر قاعدة بيانات تحصر المخابز العاملة والمتوقفة في ولاية الخرطوم، عقب استعادة السيطرة على الولاية في مايو 2025م. ولفت إلى أن تطبيق أي نظام جديد لدعم الدقيق يتطلب موارد وإمكانات مالية كبيرة، مشيراً إلى أن توفير الدعم لكميات تصل إلى قرابة 200 ألف جوال يومياً في الولايات الخاضعة لسيطرة الجيش يمثل عبئاً يصعب على الحكومة تحمله في ظل محدودية مواردها. وانتقد عكاشة ما وصفه بالمعلومات غير الدقيقة بشأن استمرار توزيع الدقيق المدعوم، مؤكداً أن نظام دعم الدقيق بصورته السابقة انتهى منذ أكثر من خمس سنوات تقريباً، وأن الدقيق المتداول حالياً هو إنتاج المطاحن الذي يُوزَّع عبر وكلائها. ودعا إلى مراعاة الظروف الاقتصادية التي تمر بها البلاد، مشيراً إلى أن معالجة أزمة الخبز تتطلب تضافر الجهود، في وقت لا تزال فيه مشكلات الإمداد بالوقود والكهرباء والدقيق تلقي بظلالها على قطاع المخابز. ومنذ التاسع من أكتوبر الماضي، بدأت عدد من المخابز في ولاية الخرطوم تطبيق زيادة جديدة على أسعار الخبز، لتباع القطعة الواحدة بـ 500 جنيه، نتيجة الارتفاع المتواصل في تكاليف الإنتاج واستمرار تراجع قيمة الجنيه السوداني. ولا تتوفر حتى الآن إحصائية رسمية حديثة وشاملة تحدد العدد الكلي للمخابز في ولاية الخرطوم، في ظل تداعيات الحرب التي تسببت في خروج أعداد كبيرة منها عن الخدمة، سواء بسبب الأضرار التي لحقت بالمنشآت أو صعوبات التشغيل ونقص الإمدادات. وتشير بيانات سابقة إلى أن عدد المخابز في الولاية كان يبلغ نحو 2,860 مخبزاً قبل اندلاع الحرب، بينما أظهرت بيانات جزئية حديثة أن عدد المخابز المصرح لها بالعمل في محلية الخرطوم بلغ نحو 275 مخبزاً، وفق توجيهات للمحلية في سبتمبر 2026م، وهو رقم يخص المحلية وحدها ولا يمثل إجمالي المخابز في الولاية. وتواجه المخابز تحديات تشغيلية متزايدة، أبرزها نقص الوقود والكهرباء وإمدادات الدقيق، ما ينعكس على انتظام الإنتاج واستقرار توفير الخبز للمواطنين. الكلمات: أزمة التقرير أوقعت تلك الهجمات 484 مدنيا بين قتيل ومصاب، وأسفرت عن مقتل 176 مجندا بالجيش (رويترز) استمع 4:44 0:00 4:44 3:34 الملخص المزيد من التفاصيل اتهم مجلس السيادة السوداني إثيوبيا بإطلاق 187 طائرة مسيرة استهدفت مدنيين ومرافق حيوية داخل أراضيه. أسفرت الهجمات بحسب تقرير رسمي سوداني عن مقتل وإصابة مئات المدنيين والعسكريين واستهداف بنى تحتية. قال مجلس السيادة السوداني، اليوم الأحد، إن أكثر من 180 طائرة مسيّرة هاجمت السودان خلال العام الجاري، انطلقت من داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية. وأكد مجلس السيادة الانتقالي الذي يرأسه قائد الجيش الفريق أول عبد الفتاح البرهان رصد "70 هجوما" بين فبراير/شباط وأكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2026 من "مناطق إطلاق إثيوبية" تتضمن "187 طائرة مسيّرة". وأعد التقرير وزارة الخارجية السودانية بالتعاون مع الاستخبارات العسكرية والاستخبارات العامة. وبحسب التقرير أوقعت تلك الهجمات 484 مدنيا بين قتيل ومصاب، وأسفرت عن مقتل 176 مجندا بالجيش، في النيل الأزرق والخرطوم وغيرهما، مستهدفة مستشفيات، ومناطق سكنية، ومرافق للوقود والكهرباء. المسيّرات في قلب القتال ويتصاعد التوتر بين السودان وإثيوبيا على خلفية القتال بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع، إذ يتهم الجيش السوداني أديس أبابا بالوقوف إلى جانب قوات الدعم السريع، التي يقاتلها منذ عام 2023. من جانبها تتهم أديس أبابا الخرطوم بدعم متمردي إقليم تيغراي . ويعتمد طرفا الحرب في السودان بشكل كبير على الطائرات المسيّرة ، إذ تراجعت حدة المواجهات المباشرة وارتفعت وتيرة الهجمات الجوية في الغرب والجنوب. وحذّرت الأمم المتحدة من ارتفاع وتيرة هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة التي تسببت في مقتل أكثر من 1100 شخص منذ بداية العام، بينهم أكثر من 300 خلال الشهر الماضي فقط. وحمّلت الخرطوم في التقرير "إثيوبيا المسؤولية الدولية عن العمليات العابرة للحدود" مطالبة "بالوقف الفوري للهجمات التي تُشنّ ضد أراضيها، وإغلاق المنشآت الإثيوبية التي تُستخدم من قِبل قوات الدعم السريع". وأكد التقرير أن السودان يسعى إلى "المساءلة والحصول على تعويضات عن الأضرار والدمار الناجم عن تلك الأعمال". وذكر التقرير هجوما استهدف عائلات نازحة في ود الماحي بولاية النيل الأزرق الشهر الماضي، مسفرا عن مقتل 30 مدنيا، بينهم 26 امرأة و4 أطفال. أدلة التقرير واعتمد التقرير على أدلة من حطام المسيّرات وبيانات الرحلات الجوية والسجلات العسكرية. ومن بين الأدلة حاسوب تحكم خاص بإحدى المسيّرات التي سقطت في الدمازين في النيل الأزرق في سبتمبر/أيلول، ضم بيانات مسار الطائرة التي تشير إلى انطلاقها من نقطة على عمق 1.7 كيلومتر داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية. ومنذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، يخوض الجيش السوداني و"قوات الدعم السريع" حربا اندلعت إثر خلافات بشأن توحيد المؤسسة العسكرية، وأسفرت عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص، وسط تفاقم المجاعة والأزمة الإنسانية في البلاد. وتسببت هجمات في الآونة الأخيرة على محطات الكهرباء بمناطق سيطرة الجيش في انقطاع واسع للتيار بولايات الخرطوم، ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence 🔇Unmute By Staff Writer November 1 , 2026 (ENA) Ethiopia’s announcement of the acquisition of advanced Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to receive S-400 air defence systems marks a significant development in the country’s efforts to modernize its national defence capabilities, strengthen the protection of its airspace and reinforce its strategic deterrence. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced on October 28 in Moscow, Russia that Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first batch of Su-35 fighter jets under an agreement with Russia and would also receive four batteries of the S-400 air defence system. He described the development as a major milestone in the country’s efforts to strengthen national security, safeguard sovereignty and contribute to regional stability. The announcement, made during the Prime Minister’s visit to Moscow for the Third Russia–Africa Summit, also underscored the growing defence cooperation between Ethiopia and Russia. Beyond Military Acquisition: A Strategic Investment in National Security The acquisition represents more than the addition of advanced military equipment to Ethiopia’s arsenal. It reflects a broader effort to build a modern defence force capable of responding to evolving security challenges and protecting the country's national interests. The Su-35, a fourth-generation-plus multirole fighter, is designed to undertake air-superiority and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, manoeuvrability and weapons systems provide capabilities for airspace surveillance, interception and a range of combat operations. The planned acquisition of the Russian-made S-400 system would add another dimension to Ethiopia’s air defence architecture. Designed to engage aircraft, cruise missiles and other aerial threats, the system is intended to provide long-range air defence capabilities and strengthen the protection of strategic assets. Together, these platforms could expand Ethiopia’s capacity to monitor and defend its airspace. However, their effectiveness will depend not only on the equipment itself but also on trained personnel, maintenance systems, logistics, command-and-control infrastructure and the ability to integrate different defence capabilities. Deterrence as an Instrument of Peace The strategic significance of military modernization extends beyond battlefield capabilities. A credible defence posture can serve as a deterrent by raising the potential costs of aggression and discouraging threats before they escalate into conflict. Prime Minister Abiy has emphasized this principle, noting that military preparedness is not simply about fighting wars but also about preventing them. For Ethiopia, strengthening defence readiness is closely connected to protecting its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national development interests. The objective, as articulated by the government, is to build the capacity to safeguard peace and security while reducing vulnerability to external threats. This approach places deterrence within a broader national security framework in which military preparedness is intended to support stability rather than confrontation. Regional Security and the Horn of Africa Ethiopia’s defence modernization carries significance beyond its national borders, particularly given its strategic position in the Horn of Africa and its extensive economic and security interests across the wider Red Sea region. As a landlocked country with a large population and substantial dependence on regional trade and transport corridors, Ethiopia has important interests in the security of its airspace, critical infrastructure and cross-border economic connections. The evolving security environment in the Horn of Africa, together with the growing use of drones, precision-guided weapons and other emerging military technologies, has increased the importance of modern surveillance, air defence and rapid-response capabilities. In this context, Ethiopia’s investment in advanced fighter aircraft and air defence systems reflects an effort to adapt its defence posture to changing regional and technological realities. At the same time, military modernization alone cannot guarantee regional stability. Sustainable peace also requires diplomatic engagement, confidence-building, respect for national sovereignty and stronger regional cooperation. A credible deterrent is most effective when complemented by constructive relations with neighbouring countries and regional institutions. Building a Modern and Sustainable Defence Force The acquisition of advanced platforms also places greater importance on the institutional and technological foundations of national defence. Operating sophisticated fighter aircraft and integrated air defence systems requires specialized training, reliable maintenance facilities, technical expertise, secure supply chains and sustained investment in personnel development. The Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) has made significant strides in expanding its military capabilities through the acquisition of modern and sophisticated weaponry, reflecting an ambitious effort to transform its defence posture. Beyond conventional military capabilities, the ENDF is increasingly moving towards a technology-driven defence model, seeking to integrate artificial intelligence, cyber operations, digital warfare and advanced surveillance technologies into its military operations. This transition reflects the changing nature of modern warfare, where technological superiority, real-time intelligence and integrated command-and-control systems are becoming increasingly important. However, building a modern and technologically advanced military requires more than acquiring sophisticated weapons systems. It also demands sustained investment in specialized training, technical expertise, maintenance infrastructure, logistics, research and development, and institutional capacity to operate and sustain these capabilities over the long term. Strengthening these foundations will be essential to translating military modernization into lasting operational readiness and strategic self-reliance. The development also highlights the importance of strengthening domestic technical expertise and reducing dependence on external support wherever possible. Building such capabilities is essential to ensuring that military modernization translates into sustainable national defence readiness. Sovereignty, Security and the Pursuit of Peace Ethiopia’s latest defence acquisitions form part of a broader national effort to strengthen its security institutions and respond to an increasingly complex regional environment. The delivery of the Su-35 fighter jets and the planned arrival of the S-400 systems signal an expansion of the country’s defence ambitions and its military cooperation with Russia. Ultimately, the significance of this modernization will be measured not simply by the sophistication of the equipment acquired, but by the country's ability to translate those capabilities into effective national defence, strategic resilience and a more secure regional environment. For Ethiopia, the central objective remains the protection of sovereignty and the preservation of peace. A modern, capable and sustainable defence force, complemented by diplomacy and regional cooperation, can play an important role in safeguarding national interests and creating the security conditions necessary for long-term development. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

Announced by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed during his visit to Moscow for the Third Russia–Africa Summit, these developments aim to enhance national security, protect airspace, and reinforce strategic deterrence. The Su-35, known for its advanced capabilities, will significantly improve Ethiopia's air superiority and combat operations. The S-400 system will bolster long-range air defense, addressing evolving regional security challenges. This modernization reflects Ethiopia's commitment to building a capable defense force that can respond to threats while promoting peace and stability. However, effective implementation will require trained personnel, maintenance infrastructure, and integration of advanced technologies. Ultimately, Ethiopia seeks to safeguard its sovereignty and foster regional cooperation, emphasizing that military preparedness is essential for preventing conflict and ensuring long-term national development.

Published 21 hours ago on November 1, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk A speaker reads a statement alongside two other men during an apparent Alliance for Survival press briefing. Photo credit: TMC/ Screenshot & Illustrated by Kulu Media The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a coalition of armed and political opposition groups, has issued a new statement calling for coordinated action against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and outlining its position on Ethiopia’s political and security crises. In a four-page statement dated October 31, 2026, and shared on Facebook , the coalition, also known as the Alliance for Survival, accused the federal government of deepening the country’s political divisions, prolonging armed conflicts and failing to protect civilians. The alliance argued that Ethiopia’s current challenges require fundamental political change rather than measures undertaken by the existing administration. It presented cooperation among opposition organizations and communities as central to achieving that objective. The statement blamed the government for what the coalition described as widespread insecurity, displacement, human rights violations and deteriorating economic conditions. These allegations represent the alliance’s position and have not all been independently verified. The coalition also reiterated its opposition to the current federal administration and emphasized the need for a political arrangement that would protect the rights, security and participation of Ethiopia’s different communities. Its statement called for broader cooperation among political organizations, community representatives and other groups opposed to the government. It also addressed members of Ethiopia’s security institutions, urging them to reconsider their role in the country’s political and military conflicts. The alliance has previously identified the replacement of the current government and the establishment of an inclusive transitional administration as central objectives. The latest declaration continues that political position, although it does not establish that a transition has been agreed upon or that the coalition has secured additional territory or military support. The Alliance for Survival emerged in September 2026 as a coalition bringing together organizations with different political backgrounds and regional interests, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Its formation drew attention because some participating organizations have historically pursued competing political objectives or fought on opposing sides of earlier conflicts. Their cooperation reflects a shared opposition to the federal government, but does not necessarily mean that their wider political differences have been resolved. The new statement comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, including confrontations involving TPLF-aligned forces, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF). Recent developments in Tigray have included the reported reentry of TPLF forces into Rama , followed by reports of drone strike damage in the area . The conflict has raised questions about the alliance’s military coordination and the extent to which its members can pursue a common strategy despite their differing political priorities. The declaration appears intended to reaffirm the coalition’s continued political cooperation and appeal for wider support. However, the statement does not independently establish a new joint military offensive, a formal agreement with additional organizations or a change in the balance of forces on the ground. No new response from the Ethiopian federal government to the October 31 statement had been independently verified at the time of writing. The alliance’s declaration adds to the political uncertainty surrounding Ethiopia’s continuing conflicts, although the practical implications of its latest calls remain unclear. Addressing the Third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow, Abiy said the proposed Ethiopia nuclear power plant would diversify the country’s electricity supply, which currently relies heavily on hydropower. “With Russia, we are moving toward our first nuclear power plant in line with the safety standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” Abiy said in his summit speech , published on his official YouTube channel. The prime minister said nuclear technology could also help reduce agricultural food losses and support healthcare, including cancer treatment. He emphasized that cooperation with Moscow should develop Ethiopian expertise to operate and regulate nuclear facilities. The remarks come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its electricity generation beyond hydropower, which remains vulnerable to variations in rainfall and reservoir inflows. Earlier this year, Ethiopian Electric Power reported a 20 percent reduction in water inflows linked to El Niño conditions, prompting revisions to its electricity generation and revenue targets. Ethiopia’s nuclear ambitions have been under development for several years. The country signed an intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreement with Russia in 2019, followed by additional cooperation roadmaps. In March 2026, the Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission and Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom signed a strategic roadmap covering nuclear energy development. According to World Nuclear News, Ethiopia is considering two reactors with a combined generating capacity of approximately 2,400 megawatts. However, the project remains at the planning stage, with potential sites requiring further assessment. Abiy did not announce a construction start date, final financing agreement or completion timetable during his Moscow address. The prime minister identified food security, energy and knowledge as Ethiopia’s three principal development priorities. On agriculture, he called for Russian cooperation in farm machinery and agricultural processing industries to increase domestic production and strengthen food security. He said Ethiopia wanted to move beyond producing raw agricultural commodities by expanding industries capable of processing harvested products. Abiy also announced that Ethiopia is establishing the Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa and invited Russian universities and research institutions to participate in teaching and research. “An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people,” he said, emphasizing that African institutions should determine how artificial intelligence systems use their data. The proposed university forms part of Ethiopia’s broader technological development ambitions. At the recent Tana High-Level Forum, Abiy also outlined the country’s Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy , highlighting digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and data governance as priorities for economic development. The prime minister said scientific cooperation should produce practical economic benefits rather than remain limited to academic exchanges. He invited Russian enterprises to establish joint ventures in Ethiopia’s special economic zones, particularly in pharmaceutical manufacturing and machinery production. Such investments, he said, could supply markets across Africa through the African Continental Free Trade Area. Abiy also called for improved payment arrangements between Ethiopia and Russia to make bilateral trade simpler and less expensive. His proposals came as the two countries continued expanding diplomatic, economic and military cooperation. During the Moscow summit, Abiy held bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear energy, healthcare, trade and other areas of mutual interest. The talks followed Ethiopia’s recent announcement concerning the acquisition of Russian military aircraft and air-defence equipment. On October 28, Kulu Media reported that Ethiopia announced new Russian Su-35 fighter jets amid renewed military tensions in the Horn of Africa. The latest summit discussions indicate that Ethiopia is seeking cooperation with Moscow across both civilian and defence sectors. Abiy also proposed that Addis Ababa host a future Russia–Africa Summit when the gathering next takes place on the African continent. He said the Ethiopian capital, which hosts the African Union headquarters, would be honored to welcome the meeting. However, he did not announce that Addis Ababa had been formally selected as the venue. The prime minister urged participating countries to adopt an action plan containing clear responsibilities and implementation timelines. He said international cooperation should translate diplomatic commitments into practical results. On international affairs, Abiy reaffirmed Ethiopia’s support for negotiated solutions, African-led mediation and consistent application of the United Nations Charter. His remarks came amid continuing Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions , with international partners urging restraint and diplomatic engagement to prevent a broader regional conflict. Abiy did not directly address the dispute with Eritrea in the supplied summit speech. Reflecting on historical relations, the prime minister recalled a Russian medical mission that assisted wounded Ethiopians following the Battle of Adwa in 1896. He said the mission translated a medical guide into Amharic, presenting the initiative as an early example of scientific cooperation between the two countries. Abiy also noted that his book Medemer had been translated into Russian, describing the exchange of knowledge as a symbol of the longstanding relationship. The speech concluded with a call for stronger cooperation based on sovereignty, technological capability and shared economic development. For Ethiopia, the proposed nuclear power plant, artificial intelligence university and expanded industrial partnerships represent central elements of the government’s long-term development agenda. However, the financing, construction timetable and implementation arrangements for the nuclear project remain to be finalized. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali/Facebook Ethiopia has announced the arrival of 12 advanced Russian Su-35 fighter jets, marking a major expansion of its military airpower as renewed fighting in Tigray and worsening relations with Eritrea raise security concerns across the Horn of Africa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the delivery on October 28, 2026, saying the aircraft were supplied under an existing defence agreement with Russia. He also confirmed plans for Ethiopia to receive four batteries of Russia’s S-400 air-defence system, although no delivery date was announced. According to Ethiopia’s state-affiliated Fana Media Corporation , Abiy described the arrival of the aircraft as an important step in strengthening national security and protecting Ethiopia’s sovereignty. The prime minister said Russian President Vladimir Putin had helped accelerate the delivery, allowing Ethiopia to receive the fighter jets one year earlier than originally scheduled. The announcement coincided with Abiy’s visit to Russia for the third Russia–Africa Summit, where defence cooperation has become a prominent element of relations between Addis Ababa and Moscow. The Su-35 is a Russian-built, twin-engine multirole fighter aircraft designed for air-to-air combat and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, maneuverability and weapons capabilities could expand the Ethiopian Air Force’s operational options. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Ethiopian and Russian officials pose for a group photograph in front of a fighter aircraft during a military aviation event. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali / Facebook The planned S-400 acquisition would add another dimension to Ethiopia’s military modernization. The Russian-developed system is designed to detect and engage aircraft, missiles and other airborne threats at considerable distances. However, the government has not disclosed the value of the agreement, the expected arrival date of the S-400 batteries or where the newly acquired aircraft will be stationed. In its October 28 report , Reuters said Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec had not immediately responded to a request for comment. The aircraft delivery announcement comes during a particularly sensitive period for Ethiopia’s security environment. Fighting involving the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), TPLF-aligned forces and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) has intensified in northern Ethiopia since September, while relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply. The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting TPLF-aligned forces and interfering in Ethiopia’s internal security affairs. Eritrea has rejected accusations of involvement and has made counterclaims concerning Ethiopian military intentions. Earlier this month, Ethiopia formally accused Eritrea of an invasion , alleging that Eritrean troops had advanced into northern Ethiopia. The allegations remain disputed. Ethiopian military chief Field Marshal Berhanu Jula also recently accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting TPLF-aligned forces, including through alleged weapons transfers. Those specific allegations have not been independently verified. The new aircraft could strengthen Ethiopia’s capacity to defend its airspace and conduct military operations, although their immediate operational readiness and deployment arrangements remain unknown. There is no verified evidence that the newly delivered Su-35 fighters have been deployed in the current fighting or assigned to operations against Eritrea. The acquisition nevertheless carries regional significance because Ethiopia and Eritrea remain locked in a confrontation involving border security, political alliances and Ethiopia’s long-standing interest in reliable access to the Red Sea. International concern about a broader conflict has increased. The United States recently warned of wider war , urging restraint as tensions between the two countries continued. Russia has also indicated a willingness to facilitate discussions between Ethiopia and Eritrea if both governments agree, but no confirmed bilateral negotiations have emerged from the Moscow summit. Ethiopia and Russia have maintained military relations for decades, including cooperation involving combat aircraft, defence equipment and technical training. The latest announcement signals a further strengthening of those ties at a time when Ethiopia is seeking to modernize its armed forces while navigating internal conflict and regional diplomatic pressure. For now, the confirmed government announcement concerns the delivery of 12 Su-35 fighter jets. The four S-400 air-defence batteries remain part of a future delivery commitment, with their schedule and deployment locations undisclosed. Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre. The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training. Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last. In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable. He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership. "Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both. Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives. The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia. It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has initiated military training for his cabinet ministers and senior government officials, emphasizing that such discipline is essential for effective leadership and national development. The training, conducted at the Hurso military training center, includes prominent figures like the Speaker of the House of Federation and the Finance Minister. Abiy believes that military training can instill values such as teamwork, accountability, and patriotism, which are crucial for achieving Ethiopia's goals of universal prosperity. This unusual move comes amid ongoing conflicts in the northern Tigray region and heightened tensions with Eritrea. Abiy has previously highlighted the importance of military preparedness in addressing Ethiopia's security challenges. The duration of the training remains unclear, but it reflects a strategic approach to leadership development in a country facing multiple crises.

Opposition Parties, UN Agencies Sound Alarm Over Security Incidents, Civilian Safety in Ethiopia 3 minute read By Abraham Tekle October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL UN agencies report tens of thousands fled to Kenya Opposition political parties and United Nations agencies have voiced mounting concern over civilian casualties, security incidents, and displacement across parts of Ethiopia, urging immediate measures to protect citizens, investigate reported violations, and ensure accountability amid ongoing regional violence. The Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA), in a statement issued on October 27, expressed concern that the government has fallen short of its primary obligation to ensure public safety. EZEMA also criticized public media outlets, including the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), for omitting reports of civilian casualties following incidents in the Arsi Zone of the Oromia Region earlier in the month. Detailing multiple security challenges, the party noted that violence in Arsi, alongside recurring inter-communal clashes in the past months in Gambella and Moyale, has led to loss of life, displacement, and property damage. EZEMA called on federal authorities to take proactive steps to prevent further escalations, transparently investigate institutional shortcomings, and hold responsible parties accountable. Furthermore, the party urged human rights organizations to independently examine the incidents and called for greater public media scrutiny regarding the government’s crisis response. The party appealed to federal and regional authorities to thoroughly investigate the violations, safeguard civilians, and prosecute perpetrators regardless of their official standing or political affiliation. It also encouraged international organizations, diplomatic missions, and human rights monitors to closely follow the situation, cautioning that it is prepared to organize peaceful public demonstrations under the slogan ‘Beka!’ (Enough!) if its demands for security and accountability remains unmet. Echoing these concerns, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Party (EPRP) issued a statement condemning killings, abductions, and forced displacements in the Arsi Zone, specifically highlighting Shirka and Chole districts. Citing local information, the party reported multiple deaths, injuries, and the alleged abduction of approximately 50 individuals from their homes. The EPRP advocated for an independent international investigation, the safe release of abducted persons, humanitarian assistance for displaced populations, and legal action against those culpable. These developments align with findings from the Ethiopian Human Rights Council (EHRCO), which documented a pattern of killings, injuries, abductions, and displacement across Oromia, Amhara, Gambella, and Benishangul-Gumuz in its annual human rights report covering June 2025 to June 2026. The council reiterated calls for regional and federal authorities to prioritize civilian protection and comprehensive investigations. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia’s T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia’s Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) While accountability for specific incidents remains heavily contested, Oromia Regional Government Communication Bureau Head Hailu Adugna characterized recent violence in the region as an attempt by an armed group referring to itself as ‘Tsmido’ to ignite ethnic and religious strife. Tsimdo refers to armed forces who claims to forge alliance against the government. Hailu expressed deep regret over the loss of lives and material damage resulting from the unrest. Concurrently, reports of active conflict and civilian casualties have emerged from the Amhara and Tigray regions. International media reported that drone strikes hit the Jari No. 2 displacement camp in the South Wollo Zone of the Amhara Region, resulting in a reported death toll including children—alongside numerous injuries requiring hospitalization. In the Tigray Region of Rama town, local residents reported a separate strike affecting a truck transporting sorghum, causing casualties among individuals gathered at the scene. Additional reports from October detailed airstrikes and drone activity in Adwa, Shire, and Sheraro, resulting in civilian deaths and damage to local infrastructure. The impact of the ongoing security challenges has also spilled across international borders. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), clashes near the Ethiopian-Kenyan border have prompted thousands to cross into Kenya via Moyale since October 22. Local authorities estimate that up to 50,000 individuals have crossed, with registration and verification efforts ongoing. Many of those fleeing are women and children, finding temporary shelter in local schools, churches, or with host communities. In response, the UNHCR, alongside the International Organization for Migration (IOM), UNICEF, and the World Food Programme, has launched an appeal for USD8.9 million to provide essential humanitarian assistance to up to 50,000 displaced individuals over a three-month period. The IOM indicated that humanitarian partners are actively preparing for further arrivals. Addressing the broader climate of conflict, UN Secretary-General António Guterres emphasized in a public statement that adherence to international law, addressing root causes, and pursuing political settlements remain the only viable pathways to sustainable peace. “Let’s summon the political will to silence the guns, stop the killing, and build a world where peace for all prevails,” he stated. ethiopia.content: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-31 The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia 0 Comments For a landlocked nation, maritime access is rarely a matter of simple commerce; it is an existential variable that dictates economic survival, sovereign autonomy, and strategic viability. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. As the most populous landlocked country, Ethiopia's reliance on Djibouti for 95% of its trade exposes it to significant vulnerabilities, particularly given the militarization of the Red Sea and the geopolitical tensions in the region. The recent formation of alliances among Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia aims to isolate Ethiopia, further complicating its access to vital maritime routes. This situation is exacerbated by external military presences that threaten Ethiopia's sovereignty and economic stability. Ethiopia's demand for a reliable maritime corridor is not merely an expansionist ambition but a legitimate right essential for its survival and security. The international community, alongside regional organizations, must facilitate dialogue to address Ethiopia's concerns while ensuring the interests of neighboring states are respected, to prevent potential conflict and promote regional stability.

The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Amgad Fareid Eltayeb last update on 30 Oct 2026 The dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea over the Red Sea port of Assab now extends well beyond that of a maritime facility or outlet for international trade. It reflects a structural contradiction between two states with a shared history but divided on issues like sovereignty, security, borders, and the state itself. For Ethiopia, Assab embodies its historical loss of direct access to the sea. This is a growing strategic concern, with the country’s population and economy both having expanded. For Eritrea, the port is a key and inseparable part of its sovereignty, won through a long war of independence. Thus, the port mixes economic interests with domestic power struggles, regional alliances, and foreign intervention, particularly in a region already afflicted by weak state institutions and protracted armed conflicts. The modern roots of the crisis lie in Italian colonial expansion in the 19th century. Italian control of Assab began in 1869 through the Rubattino shipping company, which acquired the right to administer the port from local authorities. Administration passed to the Italian state in 1882, and Assab subsequently became part of Italian Eritrea, formally established as a colony in 1890. With the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, this was a time of intensifying European competition for ports and trade routes through the Red Sea. Italy lost control of East Africa in 1941, when Assab and the rest of Eritrea came under British occupation and administration. Following the Second World War, Eritrea’s future administration was debated. On 2 December 1950, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 390, recommending the establishment of a federation between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The arrangement came into effect in 1952. It recognised Ethiopia’s legitimate need for access to the sea, and granted autonomy to Eritrea (with its own legislative, executive and judicial institutions responsible for internal affairs) within a federation under the sovereignty of the Ethiopian Crown. The resolution did not grant Ethiopia permanent ownership of Assab as a separate sovereign possession, but it went beyond a commercial agreement between two independent states by establishing a federation with sovereign authority at the federal level, defined powers, and Eritrean autonomy. These legal distinctions remain essential to assessing the competing claims surrounding Assab today. Emperor Haile Selassie gradually undermined Eritrea’s autonomous institutions before abolishing the federal system and fully annexing the territory in 1962. A year earlier, Eritrea’s armed struggle for independence had already begun. The Ethiopian Empire fell in the revolution of 1974, and the military regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam reasserted centralised control through force. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters arrive after eight hours of walking in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 29 June 2021. Alliances and interests Opposition to his rule fostered cooperation between the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which was waging a parallel campaign to overthrow the regime. Their common struggle contributed to Mengistu’s defeat in 1991, although the alliance concealed a fundamental difference between their political ambitions: the Eritrean movement sought to establish an independent state, while the Tigrayan movement aimed to overthrow the regime and restructure power within Ethiopia. A common enemy had united them, but victory exposed their conflicting visions of statehood. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 following a popular referendum endorsed by Ethiopia’s new government, then led by Meles Zenawi, and it was recognised by the international community. Independence made Ethiopia landlocked, losing its direct access to the Red Sea. Yet this did not disappear overnight. The country continued to use Assab under arrangements agreed with Eritrea, until mounting economic, territorial and political disputes culminated in the 1998–2000 war. This ended with the Algiers Agreement, followed by the boundary commission’s ruling in 2002. Relations between the two countries remained hostile and Ethiopia shifted almost all its maritime trade to Djibouti. Subsequent demographic and economic developments have sharpened the consequences. Ethiopia now has 135 million people, a growing industrial economy, and a thirst for international trade, but with almost all its foreign trade passing through Djibouti, it depends heavily on a single transit route. Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. In a region exhausted by conflict and the collapse of state institutions, the greatest danger is that an attempt to change Ethiopia's landlocked status by force ignites another war, at a cost to all concerned far greater than any benefit its proponents hope to gain. + / - SAVE SHARE Related topics Tigray Ethiopia Eritrea Red Sea Port international trade Horn of Africa Sudan Related Articles The leaders of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea met in Alamein Egypt on 4 October to discuss regional tensions. The historical context of the dispute dates back to colonial times, with Assab symbolizing Ethiopia's loss of direct maritime access following Eritrea's independence in 1993. Ahmed Shide Mohamed was elected the Speaker of Parliament on Monday. Share Ahmed Shide Mohamed is now Ethiopia's Parliamentary Speaker. / Others By Nuri Aden Ethiopian politician Ahmed Shide Mohamed has assumed his new role as the Speaker of the House of Peoples’ Representatives after being unanimously elected by MPs. This comes as the seventh parliamentary term started on 5 October 2026. Shide, who represents the Chereti constituency in Ethiopia’s Somali Regional State, becomes the first politician od Somali origin to serve as speaker of the House of Peoples’ Representatives, according to the information provided by Ethiopian parliamentary sources. He was formally sworn in during the inaugural proceedings of the new House, in a ceremony attended by President Taye Atske-Selassie. One of his first duties was the swearing-in of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed for another five-year term. Shide most recently served as Ethiopia’s Minister of Transport and Logistics. He previously held several senior government positions, including Minister of Finance, Minister of Transport and Minister of Government Communication Affairs. He served as Minister of Finance from October 2018 before moving to the transport and logistics portfolio. Not new to governance Before joining the cabinet, Shide spent more than eight years as a state minister at the Ministry of Finance and Economic Development, where he was involved in Ethiopia’s economic cooperation, regional development and integration agenda. During his tenure in government, the 59-year-old played a role in economic reform programmes aimed at increasing private-sector participation, improving economic efficiency and supporting broader economic development. His long record in Ethiopia’s economic policymaking has also brought him recognition as one of Africa’s influential finance ministers. In 2025, Shide was recognised among the 100 Reputable Africans, highlighting his profile in African public service and economic policymaking. World Bank role Shide has also held a number of positions at regional-state level, including senior roles in Ethiopia’s Somali Regional State. He has served as a government spokesman and has been involved in regional and international development initiatives. Shide holds a Master of Arts in Participation, Development and Social Change from the Institute of Development Studies at the University of Sussex in the United Kingdom. He also holds a postgraduate diploma in Managing Rural Resources and Resource Conflicts from the Institute of Social Studies in The Hague, the Netherlands, and an MBA from the University of Greenwich in London. He earned a Bachelor of Arts in Economics from the Ethiopian Civil Service College in Addis Ababa. Upper chamber’s leadership The upper chamber, Ethiopia’s House of Federation, also elected its leadership as the seventh parliamentary term began. Muferihat Kamil was elected Speaker of the House of Federation, while Desta Ledamo was elected Deputy Speaker. Muferihat most recently served as Minister of Labour and Skills Development, while Desta previously served as Chief Administrator of the Sidama Regional State. The appointments complete the initial parliamentary leadership arrangements as Ethiopia begins the seventh parliamentary term and proceeds with the formation of the new Medemer Government. The new parliamentary leadership is expected to oversee the legislative work of the two federal chambers during the first working year of the seventh parliamentary term.
